- Fixed freezes and runaway memory use in most cases while a hook prints output without end

- Fixed the terminal freezing, and ignoring Ctrl+C, while a local MCP server floods its standard output
- Fixed a freeze when a prompt or piped input holds an `@` followed by a very long unbroken string, such as minified CSS with an embedded font

- Fixed CLAUDE.md and rules files being sent to the model a second time, in most cases, after a session moves into a worktree under `.claude/worktrees` with EnterWorktree or is resumed there
- Fixed tool calls that never ran being counted as done in a claude.ai chat's summary line after you declined a permission prompt in a session that had restarted

- Fixed resuming a session and `/stats` freezing for seconds when a transcript holds many damaged lines

article.title: Pax: the Pydantic AI coding agent for your terminal
article.text:
Pydantic AI Harness has come a long way since we launched it alongside Pydantic AI v2 in June. It's the official capability and harness library for Pydantic AI, with more than 100 capabilities you can add to any agent.
We're getting ready to call it 1.0 in about a month, and start maintaining the same version policy as Pydantic AI. That means this is the best time to stress test it and let us know if there's still anything we should change before the public API gets set in stone for a while.
Along with that, we're releasing Pax (pydantic-ai-pax), the official Pydantic AI coding agent for your terminal, built on the Harness SDK. Just as everything in the Harness is a capability, everything in Pax is a plugin: the coding agent itself, sandboxes, MCP, Logfire tracing, and your own. And you can bring your own harness: point Pax at any Pydantic AI agent with --agent. In single runs of Harness-Bench SWE81, it had the highest average score of the four harnesses that ran all eight models, narrowly. It cost less than half of what Codex did on GPT-6.2 Sol, and about the same as Claude Code on Claude Opus 5.5.
If you try it out, please let us know what you think in our Slack.
What is what?
Pydantic AI is the agent framework: the loop, models from every major provider, tools, and structured output. For reusable building blocks on top of that core, you pass Capabilities: bundles of tools, instructions, and hooks you can add to an agent.
Pydantic AI Harness is a library of production capabilities we've built so you can assemble a harness for your own use case. Built in: durable execution that survives crashes and restarts (for agents built on the SDK; not in Pax yet), one workspace API across your machine and a dozen cloud and local sandboxes, computer use on each provider's native tool, model fallback that also catches refusals, and code mode. Plus the table stakes: file and shell tools, guardrails, memory, sub-agents, context management and Agent Skills.
One of those capabilities is Coder(), our coding harness. What the industry calls a coding harness is, in Pydantic AI, just a capability (technically a bundle of capabilities that turns any agent into a coding agent).
Pax is the terminal UI in front of Coder(). Think of it as both a daily-driver coding agent and a showcase of what you can build on the Harness SDK: bring your own agent with --agent, swap sandboxes on the fly, and run any model.
Everything is a plugin
A Pax plugin is just a capability one layer up: tools and hooks for the agent, plus terminal pieces like /commands, status-bar items, and logins.
Even the coding agent itself is a plugin. Open /plugins to toggle coder, sandbox, observability (Pydantic Logfire tracing), mcp, and the rest on or off. Turn coder off with /plugins disable coder and you have a clean chat client with no file or shell tools. Any Pydantic AI capability works as a plugin by its import path, and Pax can even write new plugins for itself when you ask. See the Pax plugins docs.
Bring your own agent with --agent
Plugins extend Pax's default agent. --agent replaces it with any Pydantic AI Agent from your codebase:
# my_agents.py
from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.capabilities import LocalWorkspace
from pydantic_ai_harness import Coder
reviewer = Agent(
'openai:gpt-6.1-sol',
instructions='You review diffs against our internal engineering guidelines.',
capabilities=[LocalWorkspace('.'), Coder()],
)
@reviewer.tool_plain
def get_guideline(topic: str) -> str:
"""Look up an internal engineering guideline by topic."""
...
pax --agent my_agents:reviewer
pax -a my_agents:reviewer -p "Review the diff on this branch against our guidelines"
Pax loads no plugins and runs your agent as-is with its own model, tools, and instructions (here Coder()'s file and shell tools in the current directory, plus your guideline lookup), while giving you the full terminal (--resume, --worktree, -p, and -m). Build an agent in your repo, test it in a real terminal, and ship…

## 1.5.18
- Fixed the agent attaching truncated or corrupt images to the conversation when viewing files; it now rejects them with an error, so a half-written image no longer makes later model requests fail and retry.
- Fixed plugins not loading on Windows when your workspace is on a different drive than your Antigravity configuration directory.
- Fixed file permission rules and approval prompts not applying to files the agent reads or edits through `file:///` URIs; those paths now resolve to the real file before permissions are checked.
- Fixed copying from code blocks and from raw Markdown or code file views in the Remote Control browser view dropping blank lines, so pasted text keeps its original spacing.
- Fixed LaTeX equations in subagent replies showing as raw TeX in the Remote Control browser view; they now render as formatted math like the rest of the conversation.
- Fixed shell variables in chat text in the Remote Control browser view, such as `cp $src_dir/$name .` or `http://$host:$port/api`, being rendered as LaTeX math; they now show as plain text and links keep their correct addresses.
- Fixed the model quota section of the Remote Control browser view's settings spinning forever when quota fails to load; it now shows an empty state or the last known quota, and `Refresh` works again.

article.text:
# Prospero: a bloat-free, native AI coding harness with ImGui
Prospero is a native GUI application for Windows, macOS, and Linux that
connects to an AI model provider, local or remote, allowing AI agents to
drive your computer to develop software. It plows through intermittent
errors and keeps at its task while unattended. It speaks the OpenAI Chat
Completions API, used by llama.cpp, vLLM, LiteLLM, and providers with a
compatible API. Also Anthropic's Messages API, with extended thinking and
prompt caching. No providers are configured out of the box.
The UI is highly flexible, and you can rearrange the panes as you please
with dragging and docking. Save your layouts for later in View -> Layouts.
Unlike conventional ImGui applications, rendering is passive and will not
consume resources while idle.
It is a single executable, written in C++. In the typical case the engine
runs in the same process as the window, and needs no daemon or server. The
same executable can run headless, on another machine over ssh, or in the
background after its window closes. The engine is lean and portable, and
runs on computers and operating systems a quarter century old. Imagine a
coding harness on Windows XP.
Once it's connected to a provider, **you can ask Prospero for help with
itself**. It will read its own embedded documentation, self-configure, and
navigate you to any place in its UI.
Prospero's desktop control features allow it to effectively develop, test,
and debug native GUI applications. On Windows, it especially works well in
[w64devkit][], making use of its shell and tools if available.
You can start new sessions from the command line, even if there's already
an instance, by invoking Prospero with a path where the new session will
be rooted. For example, to start a session here:
$ prospero .
After no arguments, this is the second most common way to run Prospero.
## Documentation
- [Usage](docs/usage.md): running it, sessions, the GUI, attachments,
modes and the command line
- [Configuration](docs/configuration.md): `prospero.ini`, endpoints,
models, roles, instructions, skills, MCP servers and web search
- [Desktop control](docs/desktop.md): letting the agent see and drive
the screen
- [Remote and background hosts](docs/remote.md): engines on other
machines over ssh, and sessions that outlive the window
- [Windows notes](docs/windows.md)
- [Building](docs/building.md): building from source, and releases
- [Development](docs/development.md): tests, and evals for comparing
models
Prospero also carries its own documentation, under Help, which an
agent in it can read too.
## License
Prospero is free and unencumbered software released into the public
domain. See [UNLICENSE](UNLICENSE).
Its programs include third-party code under its own licenses: Dear
ImGui (MIT), FreeType (FTL), md4c (MIT), SDL3 (zlib), cpp-httplib
(MIT), Mbed TLS (Apache-2.0), and Wuffs (Apache-2.0 or MIT, at your
option), which every program with the engine includes. The built-in
model's network, `src/gemma.cpp`, is derived from gemma4.c and stays
under its MIT license.
[w64devkit]: https://github.com/skeeto/w64devkit

# enhance-qa
**A QA team for any app, inside your coding agent.**
A scout maps your app, testers use it the way real people do, a verifier double-checks every bug, and a fixer repairs what's clearly broken, one tested commit at a time.
How it works Any kind of app Get started What you get Results FAQ
## How it works
You stay the product owner: you confirm the plan, make the judgement calls and decide when to ship. The lead plans each pass and briefs the team, and each role does one job.
It tests every function a person can reach (every screen, control, setting, command and error) and reports only what's broken. That means things that break a promise your app makes, or do real harm. Feature requests and nice-to-haves are never filed.
| Role | What it does | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| **Scout** | Maps the product, then writes the checklist (one file per area) and app notes | Testers never rediscover your app |
| **Testers** | Use the app black-box, like people do, several at once, with evidence | Finds what your users would hit |
| **Verifier** | A fresh agent that reproduces every bug and re-checks every fix | No false alarms, and no "fixed" that isn't |
| **Fixer** | Fixes one bug per commit, with a failing test first, including other places with the same mistake. Each commit says how it was checked. It can't edit the checklist or close its own bugs | Fixes you can trust, and undo |
| **Lead** | Picks the pass, the models and the budget, keeps the record and writes your summary | One clear report instead of noise |
Every run builds on the last: only what changed gets re-tested, fixed bugs get regression checks, and a release pass ends in a go/no-go report.
**It stays out of your way:**
- **Only these stop and wait for you:**
- the kickoff on the first run;
- a one-line OK before an unusually large run;
- a pace check, only if a pass is running far longer than it said: keep going, high-risk first, or stop and resume next time;
- the go/no-go decision.
Everything else collects in one "needs you" list.
- **It fixes serious bugs during a pass,** one commit each. The rest wait until you say `/enhance-qa fix`, or go to your own coding agent with a ready prompt. It always asks before anything that changes how your app behaves, looks or reads, and before touching data, auth, payments or dependencies.
- **It learns from repeats.** When the same kind of bug shows up twice, it proposes a one-line rule for CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, or a lint rule, so your coding agent stops making that mistake. Nothing is added without your OK.
- **It never pushes,** rewrites history or deploys.
- **Run it beside your work:**
- in a second session (`claude -w qa`, or a Codex worktree chat);
- or in the background (`claude --bg "/enhance-qa"`, `codex exec --worktree`).
## Works with any kind of app
If you can run it, enhance-qa can test it. It picks the right checks for what you're building from a library of 22 platform modules, 24 feature packs and 16 release gates.
| Area | What it covers |
|---|---|
| **Web** | Web apps, websites and content, browser extensions |
| **Mobile** | iOS, Android, React Native, Flutter and Expo |
| **Desktop** | Windows, macOS, Linux, Electron and Tauri |
| **Developer tools** | CLIs, APIs and backends, libraries and SDKs, data pipelines |
| **Games and creative** | Games, audio plugins, XR, plugins for apps like VS Code, Figma, JetBrains IDEs and Office |
| **AI and devices** | AI and LLM features, chat bots, embedded and IoT devices, TV and media deliverables |
| **Feature packs** | Sign-in, payments, accessibility (WCAG 2.2 AA), security, privacy, languages and right-to-left text, uploads, search, offline sync, notifications and more, plus a pack for the defects AI-built apps tend to have: open Supabase or Firebase data, broken authorisation, leaked secrets, features that only look finished |
| **Release gates** | App Store, Google Play, Microsoft Store, Steam, Xbox, console checklists you…

article.title: OpenAI may be in cost control mode | micjm
article.text:
OpenAI may be in cost control mode
2026-11-26
OpenAI’s recent release of Astra 6.2 and Sol 6.2 was widely panned. What happened?
Based on our data, it looks like they’ve been tuned for cost savings. Specifically output tokens per task and reasoning tokens per task have dropped.
Here is a chart of high-level cost change from the GPT-6 to GPT 6.2:
The X axis in the above chart is the ratio of spending of the GPT model compared to opponents in our battle system for real work. The Y axis on the above chart is Elo from our leaderboard.
The moves in the chart are significant, here’s the same chart with confidence intervals:
What changed
Compared to opponents, Astra and Sol seem to be reasoning a lot less. Here is a chart of how much models reason compared to opponents in the same battle. Above the line means more reasoning and below means less.
You can see that both Astra 6 and Sol 6.1 were pretty normal models, but Astra 6.2 and Sol 6.2 become outliers.
We can see the same effect with output tokens:
Are these changes significant? The p-value on output dropping is 0.0055 for Sol and 0.022 for Astra. The p-value on reasoning dropping is 0.00013 for Sol and 0.0064 for Astra.
In conclusion, Astra and Sol appear to be cost tuned compared to their predecessors, and to a degree that makes them underthinking outliers.
